title: Thymic mass in an elderly male patient with myasthenia gravis: A rare presentation
case_prompt: A 70-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of bilateral eyelid drooping, double vision, and eye watering. Initially, eye watering was sudden in onset, progressive, worsened with eyelid rubbing, and improved with cold-water eye washes. Blurring of vision with diplopia developed in the right eye, followed 8 days later by sudden, progressive right-eyelid drooping, reaching complete ptosis within 10 days. After six weeks, blurring and drooping occurred in the left eye, accompanied by periorbital edema. He also noted breathlessness on walking a few steps. He had no history of hypertension, diabetes, or other systemic illness. On examination, there was complete bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and restricted extraocular movements. Bulbar muscle fatigability was demonstrated on the SLURP test. Application of an ice pack to the eyelids produced a 3 mm improvement within 5 minutes, indicating a positive ice pack test. Generalized examination revealed areflexia. A chest x-ray showed a well-defined, lobulated radio-opaque lesion in the right hemithorax adjacent to the mediastinum. High-resolution CT of the thorax revealed a well-defined, round to oval soft-tissue density lesion in the anterior mediastinum—predominantly on the right—partially obliterating the retrosternal space and compressing the lateral border of the right atrium, suggesting a thymic mass.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Thymic adenoma was considered based on the CT appearance of an anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass — “suggesting it to be a thymic mass, which includes differentials of thymoma, and thymic adenoma.”  
2. Thymic cyst was a possibility because cystic changes can mimic thymoma on imaging — “Histopathologically, cystic changes are associated with thymoma in about 40% of the population. These cysts can be small or can be large enough to appear as a thymoma.”  
3. Thymic hyperplasia was less likely in this elderly patient due to age-related involution of the gland — “With advancing age, the cellular element of the thymus starts to decrease, and fatty infiltration starts to replace the normal glandular tissue... involution of the thymus, which is completed by the age of 60 years.”  
4. Thymoma was confirmed as the diagnosis by histopathology demonstrating epithelial cells and Hassall’s corpuscles — “The lesion was confirmed to be a thymoma on histopathology (Fig. 3).”
